title: Minimum Cost to Make Arrays Identical
summary: Given two integer arrays, arr and brr, both of length n, and an integer k, you can perform the following operations on arr: - Split arr into any number of contiguous subarrays and rearrange these subarrays in any order.
statement: Given two integer arrays, arr and brr, both of length n, and an integer k, you can perform the following operations on arr: - Split arr into any number of contiguous subarrays and rearrange these subarrays in any order. This operation incurs a cost of k. - Choose any element in arr and add or subtract a positive integer x from it. The cost of this operation is x. The goal is to make arr identical to brr with the minimum total cost.
constraints: arr and brr have equal length up to 100,000; k is nonnegative.
Without rearranging, changing arr[i] to brr[i] costs their absolute difference.
Alternatively pay k once to reorder arbitrary contiguous pieces, which permits any permutation; return the cheaper total.
known_wrong_solutions:
def minimum_identical_array_cost(arr,brr,k):
    direct=sum(abs(left-right) for left,right in zip(arr,brr))
    reordered=k+sum(abs(left-right) for left,right in zip(sorted(arr),sorted(brr)))
    return reordered
def minimum_identical_array_cost(arr,brr,k):
    direct=sum(abs(left-right) for left,right in zip(arr,brr))
    reordered=k+sum(abs(left-right) for left,right in zip(sorted(arr),sorted(brr)))
    return direct
hints: Paying the rearrangement fee allows every element to be matched to any target position.
Compare direct positional cost with sorted-to-sorted minimum absolute matching plus k.
Compute both totals and return their minimum.
For absolute distance on a line, uncrossing any inverted pair never increases cost, proving sorted matching is optimal.
